genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman running the restoration site grew up beside a wetland
her father taught her how to turn the peat
she had noticed the decline of the birds that bred there
she trained at a university in ecology
her first crew replanted bare banks
the young trees set too deep in the soil died off
she then picked species that tolerate standing water
the passing birds came back once the reed cover closed over
she passes her method on to crews from elsewhere
she says a damaged habitat is healed by patience and not by machine power
text: The woman who now runs the restoration site grew up a short walk from a marsh. Her father put a spade in her hands early and showed her how to turn the peat. She watched the brackish water rise and fall each year, and she kept count of the nesting birds as their numbers thinned. Ecology at the university came next. Her first crew was sent to replant stripped banks, and the work failed: the saplings went in too deep and rotted in the sodden ground. So she changed the approach, picking species that shrug off standing water and setting the holes farther apart. Many seasons on, the reed bed has closed over itself and the passing flocks are back. She trains crews who come from other regions now, and she tells them the same thing every time: a broken habitat mends through patience and close watching, never through the force of machines.

units: the narrator finds the shared compost yard worth attention
the rules of the yard turn away thick woody stems
a shredding machine was therefore brought in
waste reduced to chips breaks down twice as fast as before
the number of people using the yard has risen
the noise of the machine disturbs the ground floor homes
the compost is not screened before it is handed out
users therefore carry home useless bits of wood
the quality of the product changes from one bin to another
the writer holds that a screen would correct most of the flaw
text: Honestly, the shared compost yard is worth a look, even if the running of it limps in places. Whole branches are not allowed in the bins, so somebody had to bring in a shredder, and that machine is what changed everything: chipped up, the scraps break down in one season instead of two. Word got around, and now people show up with their buckets and wait their turn. The catch is the racket. The motor screams, and the folks on the ground floor keep their windows shut all morning. Someone also told me the finished compost ought to be screened before it goes back out, or gardeners walk off with lumps of wood they cannot use. That step simply does not happen, so what you get depends on which bin you dig into. My verdict is short: fine idea, sloppy execution, and one screen away from being a model of its kind.

units: the writer is staying at a water treatment works
the incoming water carries nitrogen compounds
the level climbs after rain falls on the neighboring crops
the metal pipes suffer chemical attack
the repairs are expensive
a planted wetland was laid out upstream
the plants clean the water before it reaches the tanks
the pollutant load drops by about a third
the power use of the works falls as well
the crew intends to enlarge the filtering area
text: I am writing from the treatment works where I am spending the week, and what goes on here should catch your interest. The intake basin takes in water loaded with nitrates, and the readings climb as soon as rain washes off the fields next door. That worries the operators, because the metal piping has started to corrode and every repair costs a fortune. What surprised me was how plain the answer is. Upstream of the works, someone dug a shallow pond and planted it thick with reeds, and those plants scrub the water before it ever reaches the tanks. The load comes down by roughly a third, and the power bill has eased along with it. No extra pump, nothing added. The crew is already talking about stretching the filter pond out toward the meadow. The rest can wait until my return, so keep an evening free for me.

units: the text sets the lack of water against too much water in a river
the nature of the ground decides the answer
silty ground holds back the rising water then releases it slowly
a slope stripped of plants sheds the water at once
the specialists do not clearly name the worse of the two
the rising water lays down feeding deposits despite the damage it does
the lack of water hardens the surface and squeezes the roots
the specialists rule out hard structures and deep wells
they call for land that mixes water holds plant barriers and soils that drink
text: Which should we fear more, a river run dry or a river out of its bed? The question keeps coming back, and the answer lies in the ground you happen to be standing on. Silty flatland drinks the flood like a sponge and gives the water back over weeks; a stripped slope throws it all downstream at once. Ask which wound heals better and the water scientists start hedging. A flood tears things loose, true, and yet it also lays down feeding silt, while drought bakes the surface hard and clamps down on the roots. So what should be built? Neither a wall nor a borehole, they answer, but a stretch of land that can swing both ways: ponds that hold, hedgerows that slow, loose soil that drinks. Only then does the comparison mean anything, since one trouble eases with a slow water table and the other with the memory of runoff.

units: a technical manager sets out the procedure to people in training
her deputy speaks after each explanation
plant waste is no longer placed under a cover layer
breaking down deep in the pile it gives off a gas that warms the air
sorting takes out the metals by magnetic pull
the plastics are separated by a jet of air
the glass passes through a moving screen
the dark liquid from the rows must be pumped off before it reaches the groundwater
a cover that lets air through holds down the smell
protective gear and a ban on working alone are imposed
text: The engineer in charge of the site walked the trainees through the procedure, and her deputy filled in the gaps after each point. She began with what has changed: green waste no longer goes under a cover layer, because breaking down deep in the pile it gives off a gas with a fierce warming effect. Her deputy took over on sorting. Magnets pull out the metal, a jet of air lifts the plastic away, and the glass drops through a shaking screen. She came back to the dark liquid that seeps under the rows, which has to be pumped off before it reaches the water table. Her deputy added a word on smell, held down by a breathable sheet and a fine spray. She closed on safety: helmet, heavy gloves, and never walking alone between the skips. The trainees asked what becomes of the rejects, and the crew promised them a look at the furnace.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first settled groups opened modest growing plots at the edge of the woods
the trees took the ground back once a group moved on
making metal called for enormous amounts of wood fuel
whole stands of trees were then removed
the slopes left without trees began to slump under the rain
official orders required cutting branches instead of felling whole trunks
the slides of earth pushed those in charge to plant the slopes again
these plantings often rested on a single species
that sameness left the woodlands open to insects
a mixture of species is now held to be the best protection
text: The earliest settled groups cut into the edges of the woods, opening clearings just wide enough to sow. Whenever a hamlet moved on, the trees crept back over the ground it had left, and the forest outlived what had been taken from it. Smelting metal changed that. It swallowed charcoal in quantities nobody had needed before, whole stands came down to feed the furnaces, and the stripped hills began to slide with every heavy rain. Rules followed. Written orders called for cutting branches rather than felling trunks, and left the coppice time to ripen. Later, alarm at the mudflows drove those in charge to plant the slopes again, usually with one species and nothing else, which left those young stands defenseless once insects found them. What has been learned since comes down to a single word: variety. A mixed hillside takes both the pests and the dry spells better.

units: part of the carbon dioxide in the air passes into the seas
this taking in changes the chemistry of the water
the sea surface turns more acid
the living things that build a chalky shell are struck first
their thinnest rims are eaten into and break down
these tiny creatures feed fish and seabirds
the weakening carries through the whole food web
warmer water holds less dissolved gas
part of the carbon therefore works its way back to the air
the shallow stretches near shore react before the rest because of farm inputs and water heavy with silt
text: As carbon dioxide builds up overhead, the sea takes in a large share of it, and what it takes in alters its chemistry. The dissolved gas forms a weak acid, and the surface water turns steadily sharper. Creatures that build a chalky shell feel it first: the shell knits together poorly, and its thinnest rims begin to eat away. Since those tiny animals feed fish and seabirds alike, a weakness at the bottom travels up through the whole food web. A second effect piles onto the first. Warmer water holds less dissolved gas, so part of the carbon that went in works its way back out to the air, and the process keeps itself going. Readings taken close to shore show that the shallow stretches shift first, because they also take in muddy runoff and the fertilizer washed off the fields behind them.

units: the shared garden came close to being given up
water sat between the rows from the first heavy rain
the young plants rotted without reaching maturity
turning the soil deeper changed nothing
the layer of clay pushed the water back up
an experienced gardener found the real cause
the runoff came from the sloping parking area
a planted ditch was cut along the edge of the plot
trees that drink water were put in and the beds were raised
the harvest of the following season was heavy
text: We came within a hair of walking away from the neighborhood garden, and the letdown stung. The first real downpour left water sitting between the beds, the whole plot turned into a swamp, and the young plants rotted where they stood. A neighbour said dig deeper, so we dug deeper; nothing came of it, because the clay underneath pushed everything straight back up. It took a retired gardener to tell us we had been looking in the wrong place: the parking area sloped, and all its runoff was landing on us. So we cut a shallow ditch along the fence, put in willows to drink the excess, and raised the beds on salvaged planks. The season after that, squash sprawled over half the ground and the lettuce finally held. We laugh about it now, about the boots stuck fast and the drowned rows.

units: the text compares two ways of handling kitchen scraps at home
the space available guides the choice
the first answer uses a ventilated container
wet material and dry material are layered in it
the mixture has to be turned once a week
the finished product appears after two seasons
the second answer means burying the scraps in a dug trench
the depth of cover keeps small animals away
the second answer costs nothing but yields nothing you can take back out
the reader is asked to measure the space and count the meals cooked at home
text: Anyone who wants to deal with kitchen peelings without handing them to the collection truck has two routes to choose from, and space is what decides between them. The first is a ventilated bin: you lay down a wet layer, then a dry one, turn the pile once a week, and at the end of two seasons you pull out something dark and crumbly. The second route is plainer still. Dig yourself a trench, tip the scraps in, and bury them under enough soil that rodents lose interest. Set side by side, the bin needs watching but hands you a soil improver ready to spread; the trench costs nothing and feeds the ground where it lies, though you will never lift a single spadeful back out. To settle the matter, measure your balcony or your plot, then count the meals you actually cook at home in a week.

units: the shore described here is retreating under the waves
the posts driven in recently already lean
the water drawn from the wells has taken on a salty taste
the salt water is moving in under the growing land
the growers have given up the most delicate crops
they are turning to hardier plants that ask for less water
the cellars suffer damp and salt eats at their walls
the yard of the school was built up higher after a flood
the residents argue over holding the shoreline or moving the houses uphill
no decision has been taken locally
text: At first light the wind drops over the seawall, and you can finally hear what this place is going through. Out front, the sea gains: every storm carries off a piece of the dune, and the posts driven in last year already lean inland. At the wells, the water pulled up tastes of salt now, a sign that the salt wedge is climbing under the gardens. Farther along, in the fields, the growers have given up on the tender vegetables and fallen back on tough varieties that ask for less water. Behind the embankment, in the cellars, damp rises and salt crust chews at the foot of the walls. At the end of the lane sits the school yard, built up higher after the last flood. And everywhere the same low talk: hold the shoreline, or move the houses up the hillside? Nobody here settles it, and nobody pretends any longer that the question is absent.
